analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-run drug plan that negotiates medicine prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; after referral to two committees and a health subcommittee in 2007, it died without a markup when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added a new option to Medicare's Part D drug benefit starting in 2009: a prescription drug plan run by Medicare itself, available nationwide. The core of the bill is that Medicare, for this plan, would have to negotiate prices directly with drug manufacturers — overriding the 2003 law's ban on Medicare interfering in drug price negotiations — and encourage cheaper therapeutic equivalents. The bill also sets up an appeals process for beneficiaries denied coverage and requires pharmacies to be paid promptly on clean claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who enroll in the new plan, who would pay a uniform national premium and get access to drugs at prices Medicare negotiated directly, instead of prices set through private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers. People whose claims are denied would get a defined appeals process, and pharmacies would get guaranteed payment windows.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer at least one Medicare-operated drug plan with a nationwide service area beginning in 2009, alongside the private Part D plans.

Overrides the section of the 2003 Medicare drug law (1860D-11(i)) that barred Medicare from interfering with drug price negotiations, and requires the Secretary to negotiate purchase prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers, using strategies similar to other federal purchasers like the VA.

Directs the Secretary to encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents where medically appropriate, and to build a formulary using comparative-effectiveness assessments by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality to reward lower-cost, higher-benefit drugs.

Charges a uniform national premium based on the plan's average actuarial cost, and guarantees an appeals process — an initial review by the Secretary plus external independent review — for beneficiaries denied non-formulary drugs deemed medically necessary.
Requires the plan to pay pharmacies' clean claims within 14 days (electronic) or 30 days (paper), with claims deemed clean and payable if not contested in time.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face direct price negotiation by Medicare for the first time under Part D. Private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that sell stand-alone Part D plans would face a Medicare-run competitor with national bargaining power.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and private drug plans

drawbacks.text: The Medicare-run plan would use a national formulary with cost-control tools like tiered copays, prior authorization, step therapy, and reference pricing, locked in for the year except for limited changes — which could mean more restrictions and paperwork for some patients than private plans that tailor their formularies.

A uniform national premium means enrollees in low-cost regions effectively help cover enrollees in high-cost regions, and a single national plan design replaces the local variation private plans offer today.

A government-run plan competing head-to-head with private plans could draw the healthiest or cheapest-to-serve enrollees toward it, potentially raising premiums for people who stay in remaining private plans (a general risk of public-option designs, not addressed in the bill text).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gain is large and concrete: direct negotiation with manufacturers and a benchmark public plan would put real downward pressure on drug prices for a benefit that has historically been delivered through private insurers at higher prices than other federal purchasers pay. The trade-offs — a more rigid national formulary and disruption to the private Part D market — are real but manageable design questions. Weighed honestly, the benefit to seniors likely outweighs the costs; the bill's bigger weakness is that it never got a hearing or markup where those trade-offs could have been worked through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees, then to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever held a markup or vote; it sat there until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry introduced the bill on October 23, 2007, with 14 original co-sponsors.
The Speaker referred it jointly to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, a dual referral that requires both committees to act before the bill can move.
In early November 2007 the bill was referred to the Health subcommittees of those committees, and the action history shows no further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill had 31 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and none of the committees took it up before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the 2003 ban on Medicare price negotiation, and the private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that run Part D plans kept the market without a Medicare-run competitor. Medicare beneficiaries, who would have gotten a negotiated-price plan option, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

for.name: Rep. Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 original co-sponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with jurisdiction over Medicare health provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after it was referred on October 23, 2007.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with jurisdiction over Medicare financing
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after it was jointly referred; the bill went to the subcommittee and stayed there.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Fought government interference in Medicare drug price negotiation throughout this period, the industry position this bill would have overridden.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 initial sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever taken to reveal a fuller breakdown.

industries.note: The bill would have forced HHS to negotiate purchase prices with manufacturers for the Medicare-run plan, ending for that plan the non-interference clause that has kept Medicare from bargaining since 2003, and would push use of cheaper therapeutic equivalents. Their loss is directly seniors' savings, so their interest in the bill ran against beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Private Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: A Medicare-operated plan with national bargaining power would have competed with the private stand-alone drug plans that deliver Part D today, threatening their enrollment and margins. Keeping the Medicare-run plan off the market preserved a structure in which beneficiaries pay more than other federal purchasers pay for the same drugs.

The bill required the Medicare-run plan to pay clean claims within 14 days (electronic) or 30 days (paper), a prompt-payment guarantee pharmacies historically lack under private drug plans, where slow payment squeezes their cash flow.
